title: The Enchanted Castle
description: Published in 1907 and Nesbit's most inventive fantasy: a magic ring, a castle, a sleeping princess and a very practical dinosaur, in a comedy of wishes gone wrong.
plot_or_argument: Gerald, Jimmy and Kathleen discover a castle and a sleeping princess, and a ring that makes its wearer invisible and grants wishes; the ring's magic escalates through a series of transformations until the children must use it to undo everything.
historical_context: The 1900s, the English country house, the vogue for the fairy tale, and the early cinema and its trick effects.
literary_significance: The Enchanted Castle is the most formally playful of Nesbit's fantasies and a key text in the development of the modern children's fantasy: its combination of real children, real places and uncontrollable magic is the pattern that Lewis and Rowling would follow.

title: The Wouldbegoods
description: Published in 1901 and the sequel to The Treasure Seekers: the Bastables attempt to be good, with results far worse than their attempts to be naughty.
plot_or_argument: The Bastables form the 'Wouldbegoods', a society for being good; their efforts to help the poor, to befriend the villagers and to perform good deeds produce one disaster after another, until they abandon goodness for the summer.
historical_context: The 1900s, the Victorian and Edwardian morality of self-improvement, and the holidays of the suburban middle class.
literary_significance: The Wouldbegoods is the funniest of the Bastable books and a key text in the modern children's comedy of good intentions; its satire of the Victorian good-deed literature is one of Nesbit's sharpest jokes.

title: The Phoenix and the Carpet
description: Published in 1904 and the second Psammead book: the five children find a Persian carpet that flies and a phoenix's egg that hatches into a talking bird.
plot_or_argument: The children buy a second-hand carpet which turns out to be a magic flying carpet, and with the phoenix they travel to the Persian Gulf, to a tropical island and to the future, with the usual Nesbit consequences.
historical_context: The 1900s, the Persian rug trade, the British in the Gulf, and the Victorian and Edwardian vogue for the Oriental tale.
literary_significance: The Phoenix and the Carpet is one of the finest of the Psammead books and a classic of imperial children's fantasy; its chattering phoenix is one of Nesbit's most memorable inventions.

title: The Golden Age
description: Published in 1895 and the finest English prose of the aesthetic 1890s on childhood: eight episodes narrated by children who have outgrown the nursery and watch the grown-ups with ironic distance.
plot_or_argument: The 'Olympians' — the aunts, uncles and parents — preside over a household in which the children stage romances, bury a pig, run away to an island and hold a funeral for a dead water-rat, in a series of quiet comedies.
historical_context: The 1890s, the Victorian country house, and the aesthetic movement's cult of childhood.
literary_significance: The Golden Age is the central English book of the 1890s on childhood and a key influence on the children's literature of the next century; its ironic children and its nostalgic narrator invented the tone of the modern memoir of childhood.

title: Dream Days
description: Published in 1898 and the sequel to The Golden Age, containing 'The Reluctant Dragon' and 'The Olympians'.
plot_or_argument: The volume includes the famous tale of the boy who befriends a poetry-loving dragon and negotiates a deal with St George, and the elegiac essays on the end of childhood and the departure of the Olympians.
historical_context: The 1890s, the Victorian vogue for the dragon story, and the aesthetic cult of the child.
literary_significance: Dream Days contains 'The Reluctant Dragon', one of the most perfect short stories in English for children, and its essays on the loss of childhood are the finest in the language between Lamb and the modern memoir.

title: The Wind in the Willows
description: Published in 1908 and one of the permanent books of English childhood: the river-bank world of Mole, Rat, Badger and Toad, and the comic and terrible adventures of the four friends.
plot_or_argument: Mole leaves his burrow for the river and is befriended by Ratty; the two visit Badger and become involved in the wild career of Toad, who is obsessed with motor-cars, steals one, is imprisoned, escapes, and returns to find Toad Hall occupied by the stoats and weasels; the four friends retake the house, and the book ends with the summer on the river.
principal_characters: Mole; Ratty (Water Rat); Mr Badger; Mr Toad; Otter; the gaoler's daughter; the barge-woman; the Chief Weasel; Portly
historical_context: The 1900s, the Thames at Cookham Dean, the English class structure, and the Edwardian fear of the machine.
literary_significance: The Wind in the Willows is one of the greatest English books of the twentieth century in any genre: it is at once a children's classic, a pastoral elegy for the Thames landscape, a comedy of English character and a profound meditation on home, friendship and the passing of the world, and it has never been out of print.

title: The Tale of Peter Rabbit
description: Published privately in 1901 and by Frederick Warne in 1902: the most famous picture book in English, made from a letter to a sick child in 1893.
plot_or_argument: Peter Rabbit, disobeying his mother, squeezes under the gate into Mr McGregor's garden, eats lettuces and radishes, is chased by the gardener, loses his shoes and jacket, escapes through the gate, and returns home ill.
historical_context: The 1890s-1900s, the Lake District and the Scottish countryside, the Victorian animal story, and the new colour-printed picture book.
literary_significance: Peter Rabbit invented the modern picture book and is the most successful children's book ever published in English: its combination of exact natural history, terrifying adult violence and a small hero's survival changed what a book for children could be.

title: The Tale of Squirrel Nutkin
description: Published in 1903 and the second of Potter's little books: the impertinent squirrel who teases the owl Old Brown, and the riddle-rhymes he sings on the way to the island.
plot_or_argument: Nutkin and the other squirrels gather nuts on Owl Island and pay Old Brown an offering each day; Nutkin refuses to pay and teases the owl with riddles until Old Brown seizes him and, in the end, bites off his tail.
historical_context: The 1900s, Derwentwater and St Herbert's Island, the northern squirrel and owl, and the Victorian nursery rhyme.
literary_significance: Squirrel Nutkin is the most formally perfect of Potter's books and one of the greatest picture books in English: its riddles, its island landscape and its brutal justice make it a permanent part of the children's canon.

title: The Tailor of Gloucester
description: Published in 1903 and Potter's own favourite among her books: the story of a poor Gloucester tailor and the mice who finish the mayor's wedding coat while he lies ill.
plot_or_argument: The tailor is commissioned to make a coat and waistcoat for the mayor's wedding, falls ill with only one buttonhole left to do, and the mice of his shop finish the work in the night, singing 'no more twist'.
historical_context: The 1900s, the city of Gloucester and its cathedral, the English tailoring trade, and the eighteenth-century folk tale of the elves and the shoemaker.
literary_significance: The Tailor of Gloucester is the most beautiful of Potter's books and one of the finest English Christmas stories; its Gloucester streets, its mouselore and its celebration of the craftsman made it the book she chose to be published in her own treasured edition.

title: The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck
description: Published in 1908 and one of the most beloved of the tales: the story of a duck who wants to hatch her own eggs and is nearly eaten by a fox in a feathered hat.
plot_or_argument: Jemima, whose eggs are always taken from her by the farmer's wife, is persuaded by a polite gentleman fox to lay them in his shed; the collie Kep rescues her and the eggs are eaten, but she hatches four ducklings at last.
historical_context: The 1900s, the Lake District farm, and the traditional English country lore of the fox and the duck.
literary_significance: Jemima Puddle-Duck is one of Potter's funniest and most deeply felt books, and one of the great English countryside stories for children; the fox's politeness is a permanent lesson in danger.

title: The Tale of Mr Tod
description: Published in 1912 and the darkest and most violent of the tales: the feud of the fox Mr Tod and the badger Mr Brock, and the kidnapping of the badger's son.
plot_or_argument: Mr Tod, the fox, keeps house with a family of rabbits and feuds with Mr Brock the badger; the badger's son is kidnapped, the rabbits dig a tunnel into the fox's kitchen, and the two animals destroy each other's houses in a long war.
historical_context: The 1910s, the Lake District woods and farms, and the natural history of the fox, the badger and the rabbit.
literary_significance: Mr Tod is the most complex of Potter's books and the one in which her natural history becomes a study of the violence of the wild; it is a key text for the adult reading of Potter and for the environmental reading of children's literature.

title: Plain Tales from the Hills
description: Published in Calcutta in 1888 and Kipling's first collection of prose: forty short stories of Anglo-Indian life, written for the Civil and Military Gazette and the Pioneer, which made him famous at twenty-two.
plot_or_argument: The stories move through the stations and hill towns of British India — Simla, Lahore, Dalhousie — and record the marriages, adulteries, careers and disasters of the English, told in a hard, laconic voice and with an unerring sense of the small incident that reveals a life.
historical_context: The 1880s, the British Raj, the Simla season, the Indian Civil Service and the garrison, and the Anglo-Indian press.
literary_significance: Plain Tales from the Hills invented the modern short story of colonial life and made Kipling the prose writer of the age at twenty-two: it gave English fiction a new subject, a new economy of style and a new voice, and it is the founding book of the literature of the British Raj.

title: The Jungle Book
description: Published in 1894 and one of the most influential books in the world: the stories of Mowgli, the boy raised by the wolves of the Seeonee hills, together with the animal tales of the white seal, Rikki-Tikki-Tavi and the elephants' dance.
plot_or_argument: Mowgli is adopted by Mother and Father Wolf and taught the Law of the Jungle by Baloo the bear and Bagheera the panther; he is hunted by Shere Khan the tiger, taken by the Bandar-log, and finally returns to the man-village, while the other stories follow the white seal's search for a safe island and the mongoose's war on the cobras.
literary_form: Collection of animal stories and poems
historical_context: The 1890s, the forests of the Central Provinces, the lore of the Indian jungle, and the Victorian animal story after Black Beauty.
literary_significance: The Jungle Book is the greatest English animal story of the century and one of the most influential books of the modern imagination: its Law of the Jungle, its Mowgli and its animal characters shaped the twentieth century's idea of nature and of childhood, and it is read as a parable of empire and of the feral child.

title: Barrack-Room Ballads
description: Published in 1892 and the volume that changed English poetry: ballads in the voice of the ordinary British soldier in India, sung in dialect and slang, with a rhythm learned from the music hall.
plot_or_argument: 'Danny Deever' opens with the hanging of a soldier; 'Tommy' defends the private against the civilian's contempt; 'For to Admire' and 'Mandalay' celebrate and regret the East; 'Gunga Din' honours the native water-carrier; 'The Widow at Windsor' and 'Screw-Guns' record the soldier's view of the imperial machine.
meter_and_prosody: Ballad stanzas and music-hall metres, with heavy anaphora and refrain; mimetic dialect and soldiers' slang.
historical_context: The 1880s-90s, the British army in India and Egypt, the music hall and the new popular press, and the imperial jingoism of the Jubilee years.
literary_significance: Barrack-Room Ballads broke the Victorian poetic diction and made the private soldier a subject of lyric poetry; its influence on the language of popular verse, on Hardy, on the First World War poets and on the modern ballad is incalculable, and it remains the central poetic document of the British Empire.

title: Kim
description: Published in 1901 and the finest English novel of India: the story of Kimball O'Hara, an Irish orphan in Lahore, and of his wanderings with a Tibetan lama and his education as a spy in the Great Game.
plot_or_argument: Kim, the orphaned son of an Irish soldier, meets a Tibetan lama on a pilgrimage and becomes his chela; he is taken up by the British intelligence service, is educated at St Xavier's school, and travels the Grand Trunk Road gathering intelligence, until he finds the lama again and chooses the world.
principal_characters: Kimball O'Hara; the lama; Mahbub Ali; Colonel Creighton; Lurgan Sahib; Hurree Chunder Mookerjee; the Woman of Shamlegh; Teshoo Lama; the old soldier
historical_context: The 1880s-90s, the British Raj, the Indian railways and the Grand Trunk Road, the Great Game with Russia in Central Asia, and the lama's Buddhism.
literary_significance: Kim is the finest English novel of India and one of the great novels of the twentieth century: its picture of the road, its double education of the boy and the lama, and its fusion of imperial intelligence work with Buddhist pilgrimage make it the central English text on the relation of East and West.

title: Just So Stories for Little Children
description: Published in 1902 and Kipling's book for his own children: twelve 'just so' stories of how the animals acquired their distinguishing features, told as comic fables of the earliest world.
plot_or_argument: The collection gives the whale his throat, the camel his hump, the rhinoceros his skin, the leopard his spots, the elephant his trunk, the kangaroo his legs and the alphabet its letters, and ends with 'The Butterfly That Stamped'.
literary_form: Collection of twelve tales (with the author's own illustrations)
historical_context: The 1890s, the Victorian and Edwardian nursery, the evolutionary fable, and the Brer Rabbit tradition of the animal tale.
literary_significance: Just So Stories is one of the most inventive and beloved books in English and the finest comic prose Kipling wrote for children: its invented language, its nonsense logic and its invented cosmogonies made it a permanent nursery classic.

title: Stalky & Co.
description: Published in 1899 and the most famous English school story after Tom Brown's Schooldays: the adventures of three boys at a second-rate public school and their war against the masters.
plot_or_argument: Stalky, M'Turk and Beetle outwit the masters, run their own newspaper, avenge themselves on the school bullies, and in the last story return as officers in India, where their military cunning has been formed by the school.
historical_context: The 1870s, the United Services College at Westward Ho, the Victorian public school, and the imperial officer class.
literary_significance: Stalky & Co. is the classic English public-school story and the central literary document of the education of the imperial elite; its amoral comedy and its celebration of loyalty and cunning made it the model for the modern school story and a key text in the history of English education.

title: The Story of an African Farm
description: Published in 1883 under the name Ralph Iron and the first great novel of the South African interior: the childhood and youth of three children on a Karoo farm, and the philosophical argument that is carried inside their story.
plot_or_argument: Waldo, the Boer-woman's son, Em, her daughter, and Lyndall, the orphaned English child, grow up on a sheep farm in the Karoo; the stranger Bonaparte Blenkins cheats the old Dutchwoman Tant' Sannie, the English overseer and the children's lives are shaped by the arrival of the stranger who calls himself the devil, and Lyndall goes away to school, is betrayed by a lover, and dies in a hotel room in Bloemfontein.
principal_characters: Lyndall; Em; Waldo; Tant' Sannie; Bonaparte Blenkins; Gregory Rose; the Stranger; Otto
literary_form: Novel (published under the pseudonym Ralph Iron, 1883)
historical_context: The 1860s-70s, the Karoo, the Boer farm economy, the English immigrants in the Cape, and the Victorian debate on evolution and faith.
literary_significance: The Story of an African Farm is the founding novel of South African literature and one of the great English novels of the nineteenth century: it is the first novel to make the South African landscape a spiritual place, its heroine Lyndall is one of the earliest feminists in fiction, and its allegorical 'dream' chapters are among the most original things in Victorian prose.

title: Woman and Labour
description: Published in 1911 and the most systematic work of feminist theory by a nineteenth-century English writer: a history and analysis of women's labour, and an argument for women's economic independence.
plot_or_argument: Schreiner argues that women have been historically the producers of the means of subsistence, that the industrial revolution destroyed their economic function, and that the claim for the vote and for work is a demand for the restoration of an ancient position rather than for a new privilege.
historical_context: The 1900s, the suffrage campaign, the new women's work of the 1890s, and the debate on the 'parasitic woman' that followed Lester Ward and Thorstein Veblen.
literary_significance: Woman and Labour is a founding text of English feminist theory and the most important work of its kind between Wollstonecraft and Woolf: its argument about the economic function of women shaped the suffrage campaign and the twentieth-century analysis of women's work.

title: Dreams
description: Published in 1890 and the finest of Schreiner's allegories: a series of dream-visions on hunters, strangers, women and death, written in a plain prose that has the quality of the Old Testament.
plot_or_argument: In 'The Hunter' a man pursues a wounded buck across a plain and is shown the track of the hunter who has gone before him; in 'The Woman's Rose' and 'Three Dreams in a Desert' the whole history of women is unfolded in images of a march, a river and a great wall.
historical_context: The 1890s, the vogue for the prose poem, the English reception of the Symbolists, and the allegorical tradition of Bunyan.
literary_significance: Dreams is the finest body of English allegory after Bunyan and the most original work of the 1890s: its prose poems were read as scripture by the feminist movement, and they anticipate the dream-visions of the modern short story.

title: Trooper Peter Halket of Mashonaland
description: Published in 1897 and the most direct English protest against the imperial conquest of southern Africa: the story of a trooper of the Chartered Company alone in the veld, and the stranger who comes to him.
plot_or_argument: Peter Halket, a trooper in Rhodes's Mashonaland, sits by his fire in the veld and is joined by a stranger who shows him the reality of what he has done in the name of empire, and of the hanging of a native chief; the trooper's conscience is awakened and the story ends with his death.
historical_context: The 1896-97, the Jameson Raid, the Matabele and Mashona risings, and the English debate on the Chartered Company's conduct.
literary_significance: Trooper Peter Halket is the most important English literary protest against imperialism in the 1890s and a founding text of the anti-colonial novel: it was suppressed by the circulating libraries and it marks the beginning of the literary critique of empire from within English writing.

title: While the Billy Boils
description: Published in 1896 and the founding book of Australian literature: sixty-two short pieces, most of them written in or after the year Lawson spent in the drought country around Bourke.
plot_or_argument: The stories give the bush in brief, hard anecdotes: the swagman and the squatter, the shearer and the cook, the mother and the lost child, the man who dies of thirst in the tank, the union men and the non-union men on the track.
historical_context: The 1890s, the Australian shearers' strikes, the drought of 1891-95, the Bulletin school, and the federation movement.
literary_significance: While the Billy Boils created the Australian short story and made the bush the national place: its plain speech, its laconic narrator and its refusal of sentiment shaped Australian literature for the next century, and it is the first book in which Australian English is written as it is spoken.

title: 'The Drover's Wife'
description: Published in the Bulletin in 1892 and the most famous Australian short story: a night in the life of a drover's wife alone on a selection with her children, while a snake hides under the house.
plot_or_argument: The woman keeps watch through the night with her baby and her children and the dog Alligator, barricades the room, feeds the fire, thinks of her past and of her husband away with the cattle, and kills the snake with the dog's help.
historical_context: The 1890s, the woman on the selection, the absence of the drover, and the isolation of the Australian interior.
literary_significance: 'The Drover's Wife' is the founding story of Australian literature and the classic English account of the rural woman's solitude: it has been adapted, rewritten and answered by Australian writers for over a century and is the central text of the national literary tradition.

title: Joe Wilson and His Mates
description: Published in 1901 and the most autobiographical of Lawson's books: the stories of Joe Wilson, a bushman, and of his courtship, marriage and the death of his child.
plot_or_argument: 'The Author's Farewell to the Bushmen' introduces the cycle; 'Joe Wilson's Courtship', 'Brighten's Sister-in-Law', 'A Double Buggy at Lahey's Creek' and 'Water Them Geraniums' follow Joe from youth to marriage and to the death of his son and the endurance of his wife.
historical_context: The 1890s, the New South Wales bush, the selectors and the small farmers, and the Bulletin's version of the Australian character.
literary_significance: Joe Wilson and His Mates is the finest single volume of Australian fiction of the nineteenth century and the book in which the Australian short story became an art: its story of a marriage in the bush is the most moving thing Lawson wrote.

title: In the Days When the World Was Wide
description: Published in 1896 and the most popular volume of Australian verse of the period: ballads of the bush and the road, the selector and the swagman, and the famous 'The Teams'.
plot_or_argument: The volume includes 'The Teams', 'The Fire at Ross's Farm', 'Middleton's Rouseabout', 'The Ballad of the Drover', 'Up the Country' and the title poem, all in the direct ballad metres of the Bulletin school.
historical_context: The 1890s, the Australian bush ballad, the Bulletin's nationalist programme, and the federation of the colonies.
literary_significance: In the Days When the World Was Wide is the most important volume of Australian poetry of the century and the central text of the nationalist ballad: it made the bushman and the swagman the heroes of Australian verse.
